# Predicting response to PD-1 inhibitors in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas using peripheral blood inflammatory markers

**Authors:** Ruihua Fang; Yi Chen; Bixue Huang; Zhangfeng Wang; Xiaolin Zhu; Dawei Liu; Wei Sun; Lin Chen; Minjuan Zhang; Kexing Lyu; Wenbin Lei

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Otorhinolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-Sen University, Guangzhou 510080, Guangdong, PR China | bDepartment of Pathology, The First Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-Sen University, Guangzhou 510080, Guangdong, PR China

## Abstract

Patients received pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapy shown a higher response rate compared to pembrolizumab alone.

Higher NLR and lower PLR and MLR in pretreatment prefered a immunotherapy benefit.

Dynamic increase of NLR and decrease of MLR after the ICI treatment suggested a poor immune response.

MPTC model provided a larger net benefit than the CPS marker for predicting immunotherapy response.

Keywords: Head and neck squamous cell carcinomas, Immunotherapy, Response rate, Prediction model, Progression-free survival

## Abstract

Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) treatment has the potential to induce durable disease remission. However, the current combined positive score (CPS) is insufficient accurate for predicting which patients will benefit from it. In the present study, a real-world retrospective study was conducted on 56 patients of HNSCC who received ICI treatment. Then the treatment that patient received and levels of pre-treatment blood inflammatory markers (NLR, MLR and PLR) were identified to develop a model for predicting immunotherapy response. Notably, the model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.877 (95 % CI 0.769–0.985) , providing a larger net benefit than the CPS marker (AUC=0.614, 95 % CI 0.466–0.762). Furthermore, the internal validation of the prediction model showed a C-index of 0.835. Patients with high score of the model would get improved PFS than those with low score. Therefore, the prediction model for patients with local advanced or R/M HNSCC receiving ICI treatment, which represented an better efficient prediction of immunotherapy response than CPS marker.

## Introduction

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a highly heterogeneous tumor, posing a significant challenge for clinical treatment [1]. The majority of patients are diagnosed with advanced stages of the disease, and even with aggressive surgical resection and chemoradiotherapy, 50 % of patients may still experience disease recurrence or distant metastases [2,3]. Recurrent/metastatic (R/M) HNSCC carries a poor prognosis, with a median survival rate of approximately 12 months [4]. In recent years, the emergence of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI), such as PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, has greatly improved the survival rates and quality of life, becoming a first-line treatment for patients with R/M and unresectable HNSCC [5]. However, it is important to note that only 15 %−20 % of patients benefit from the ICI treatment [6,7]. Therefore, it would be a great clinical value to precisely target the beneficiary population of ICI.

Efforts are being made to identify biomarkers that predict the response to ICI treatment, such as combined positive score (CPS) of PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden or microsatellite instability [[8], [9], [10]], but this invasive way to obtain tissues might cause treatment delay and high cost. Additionally, studies have shown that patients with negative CPS can still benefit from immune therapy [11], highlighting the importance of considering multiple factors in patient selection to optimize treatment outcomes.

Recent evidence suggests that elevated value of neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) are associated with poorer prognosis in patients receiving ICI treatment [12,13]. In HNSCC, there is increasing interest in peripheral blood inflammatory markers (such as NLR, PLR and monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR)) as the potential predictors in patients at risk of recurrence and who may benefit from ICI treatment [14,15]. These markers reflect the systemic inflammatory response and impact the immune microenvironment within tumors [16]. More importantly, monitoring the dynamic changes in NLR over time may provide additional predictive value, surpassing the limitations of imaging-based assessments [17].

In view of this, a real-world retrospective study was conducted to develop a model that could accurately predict immunotherapy response and assist clinicians in making informed treatment decisions for HNSCC patients.

## Materials and methods

### Study design and patient selection

This study enrolled patients with locally advanced or R/M HNSCC who were treated with pembrolizumab (PD-1 inhibitors) alone or in combination with standard chemotherapy at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University between December 2020 and June 2023. Patients with autoimmune diseases, other malignancies, symptomatic interstitial lung diseases, and unknown clinical outcomes were excluded from the study. The follow-up period for patients ended on June 30, 2023. PD-L1 expression was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues by immunohistochemical staining using VENTANA SP142 rabbit monoclonal antibody (VENTANA benchmark ULTRA reader) [18] and the CPS was calculated by two professional pathologists (Fig. S1). PD-L1 negative expression is defined as 0 of CPS and CPS ≥ 20 means a strong PD-L1 positivity. The Clinical Trial Number was IIT-2023–045 and the research was conducted in accordance with ethical guidelines and was approved by the ethics committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University (Approval N0:[2023]283).

### Data acquisition

The clinical parameter, including gender, age, smoking status, drinking status, tumor location, grade, CPS, R/M or not, treatment options (pembrolizumab alone or in combined with chemotherapy), and pretreatment or on-treatment (day 21 and 42 from first dose of immunotherapy) level of peripheral blood inflammatory markers were collected. These blood inflammatory markers included NLR, PLR and MLR.

### Treatment and response evaluation

All included patients received at least two infusion of pembrolizumab with the standard dose of 200 mg every 3 weeks, either in combination with chemotherapy (albumin-bound paclitaxel at 260 mg/m2 and carboplatin at AUC=5) or as a standalone treatment. Disease control was confirmed through radiologic examinations, including computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, or positron emission tomography scans, as determined by specialist physicians. PFS was defined as the time from initial immunotherapy to disease progression, death or end of follow-up. The response evaluation of PD-1 inhibitors was conducted based on the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST 1.1) guidelines and independently reviewed by two experienced radiologists. A complete response (CR) was defined as the disappearance of the targeted tumor, while a partial response (PR) was defined as a > 30 % decrease in the size of the targeted tumor (Fig. S2). Progressive disease (PD) was defined as a > 20 % increase in the size of the targeted tumor, and stable disease (SD) was defined as a status that fell between PR and PD [19].

### Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 22.0 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA) and R statistical software (version 4.1; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). A non-parametric test or chi-square test was used to compare clinical parameters and blood inflammatory markers between the responsive group and non-responsive group. The dynamic changes of peripheral blood inflammatory markers during the ICI treatment in the responsive group and non-responsive group were compared using one-way or two-way ANOVA.

The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression analysis was used to select parameters with nonzero coefficients and obtain the optimal lambda. The model was then developed, and its predictive ability and accuracy were assessed using the area under the curve (AUC) with a 95 % confidence interval (CI), calibration curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA). For model validation, the bootstrap analysis [20] of 1000 randomly resampled cohorts was conducted using R software, and the C-index was used for internal validation of the model. Kaplan-Meier analysis and the log-rank test were employed to assess PFS. Finally, a nomogram was constructed using the markers included in the model for predicting immunotherapy benefit for patients with HNSCC.

Continuous variables, such as the NLR, MLR and PLR, were divided into high and low expression by setting the median as the cut-off value. The non-normally distributed data were represented by the median (interquartile range). Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05 (two-sided).

## Results

### Patient characteristics and clinical outcomes

Out of the initial 72 patients included in the study, only 56 patients with complete clinical data, treatment information, follow-up data, and clinical outcomes were ultimately included in the final analysis. These patients were further categorized into responsive group (CR + PR, n = 36) or non-responsive group (PD + SD, n = 20), based on disease control (Fig. 1). In the Table 1, there were 15 (26.79 %) patients with R/M HNSCC, 37 (66.08 %) patients with locally advanced stage and 4 (7.14 %) patients with early stage (I-II), respectively. Among the cohort, 46 (82.14 %) patients were treated with pembrolizumab in combined with chemotherapy, while 10 (17.86 %) patients received pembrolizumab alone. There were 26.80 % patients (n = 15) showed negative expression of CPS, 46.40 % patients (n = 26) showed 1–19 of CPS, and 26.8 % patients (n = 15) showed CPS ≥ 20. The median PFS for patients in the responsive group was 9.5 months, compared to 4 months in the non-responsive group, indicating that patients who responsed to PD-1 inhibitor had a better survival outcome (P < 0.01, Table 1).

### Clinical parameters associated with immunotherapy response

Among the 56 patients, 58.93 % of patients showed PR, while only 5.36 % achieved CR. The overall objective response rate (ORR) was calculated at 64.29 % in our cohort (Fig. 2A). Furthermore, patients treated with pembrolizumab in combined with chemotherapy had a higher ORR than those who received pembrolizumab alone (73.91 % vs 20.00 %, P < 0.01; Table 1 and Fig. 2B). It was interesting to find that patients with locally advanced (not R/M) HNSCC had a better response to ICI treatment than patients with R/M HNSCC, although there was no statistical difference (69.29 % vs 53.33 %, P > 0.05; Table 1 and Fig. 2B). Similarly, there appeared to be no significant correlation between the CPS and the immune response (P > 0.05; Table 1 and Fig. 2B), which showed patients with negative CPS still had a 46.67 % (7/15) of ORR (P = 0.25; Table 1 and Fig. 2B). Our results demonstrated that immunotherapy might be beneficial to patients with negative-CPS, not just for those with CPS≥20 in HNSCC, suggesting that CPS marker could not be an accurate predictor for patients' immunotherapy response.

### Pretreatment blood inflammatory closely related to immune response

The high level of pretreatment NLR and low level of pretreatment MLR and PLR were found to be strongly associated with the better response outcomes in HNSCC patients (P < 0.01; Table 1, Fig. 2C-E). These results indicated that the pretreatment blood inflammatory markers could be used as reliable predictors of the effectiveness of immunotherapy. To further investigate the dynamic changes in blood inflammatory markers during ICI treatment, we monitored these markers before each course of immunotherapy. It showed that the NLR and MLR were significantly higher in non-responder than in the patients with response, at the 21 and 42 days from the first dose of immunotherapy (P < 0.05, Fig. 2C-D). Compared with the pretreatment level of blood inflammation markers, there showed a significantly increase of NLR and a decrease of MLR after ICI treatment in patients with non-response. Meanwhile, the dynamic increase of PLR at 21 days after treatment would have an better response to immunotherapy (P < 0.05, Fig. 2E).

### Development and validation of a response prediction model

Based on the above considerations, we aimed to develop a predictive model for immunotherapy responses in patients with HNSCC. LASSO regression analysis was used to identify the most robust response-related clinical parameters (Fig. 3A). The final model, called the MPTC model, included treatment, CPS, MLR, and PLR, had an AUC of 0.877 (95 % CI: 0.769–0.985, sensitivity=0.81 and specificity=0.85) for predicting immunotherapy response. Compared to CPS marker (AUC=0.614, 95 % CI 0.466–0.762), our MPTC model showed better predictive ability (Fig. 3B). The calibration curve and DCA curve of the MPTC model demonstrated good agreement for predicting immunotherapy response (Fig. 3C). The formula for the MPTC model was as follows: response score = −0.26216916 + (−0.02464918 * MLP status) + (−1.97953064 * PLR status) + (−1.97953063 * Treatment option) + (0.19610934 * CPS status) (Table S1). To validate the accuracy of the model, we performed bootstrap analysis, which showed a high C-index of 0.8472. In the end, a nomogram was developed (Fig. 3D) to predict the response to immunotherapy for patients with HNSCC. It was revealed that the MPTC model provided a more accurate and individualized prediction of immunotherapy response for HNSCC patients.

Patients with low model scores were notably more associated with worse survival outcomes and radiographic responses indicating PD and SD. Interestingly, this pattern was not observed in relation to the CPS (Fig. 4). This indicates that our prediction model is better suited for assessing the efficacy of immunotherapy in real-world clinical patients.

Each bar indicates one patient; (B) Patients transferred between the model score, CPS, response and survival status in the training in this cohort.*

The 1-year progression-free survival of patients was 82.7 % in our real-world data (Fig. 5A). Based on the MPTC model formula, each patient was assigned a model score, and they were divided into high-score and low-score groups using the median as a cut-off value. The results indicated that the patients with high score had an longer PFS, compared to those with low score (P = 0.03, Fig. 5B). What's more, the results showed that patients with CR or PR had longer PFS than those with SD or PD (P = 0.03, Fig. 5C). However, when analyzing patients with different CPS, no significant difference in PFS was observed (P = 0.52, Fig. 5D). Additionally, it was noted that patients treated with pembrolizumab alone, exhibited a tendency towards shorter PFS. However, this difference did not reach statistical significance (P > 0.05, Fig. 5E, F). Similarly, patients with locally advanced HNSCC preferred to have a longer PFS and overall survial (OS) compared to those with R/M, though this discrepancy was also not statistically significant (P > 0.05, Fig. S3).

## Discussion

As it is well-known, the response to immunotherapy plays a crucial role in guiding clinicians to choose the most appropriate treatment regimen. Despite the ICI treatment have shown promising clinical outcomes for R/M HNSCC patients, only 18 % of them experiencing immunotherapy response as shown in phase 1/2 KEYNOTE-012 [21]. Moreover, the KEYNOTE-048 study [22,23] and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) [24] highlighted that CPS should be considered when selecting ICI as a first-line treatment option. However, even among patients with a CPS≥20, the response rate remains relatively low at 23 %, whereas patients with negative CPS can still benefit from ICI treatment [25]. Few association between the expression of PD-L1 and the immunotherapy response had been reported [26], which was consistent with our findings. In recent years, there has been a rise in the proposal of various immunotherapy biomarkers, but it has become evident that no single biomarker can effectively predict the efficacy of ICI on its own [27]. Therefore, identifying a more simplified and cost-effective diversified model for optimizing and personalizing immunotherapy response is crucial.

Previous studies had strict and complex enrollment criteria, leading to limited representation of real-world patients. The current prediction model for response to immunotherapy shown in many clinical studies was only for the patients with R/M HNSCC [28,29], and the predictive efficacy for locally advanced patients is unknown. To the best of our knowledge, this was the first report of a predictive model for immunotherapy response in HNSCC based on a real-world clinical data. A recent meta-analysis of current clinical trials reported that the patients who received neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy had a higher ORR, compared to patients receiving immunotherapy alone in HNSCC (ORR: 61 % vs 22 %) [30]. In our retrospective cohort, we observed an ORR of 64.29 % and a median PFS of 8 months in HNSCC patients. The ORR results were higher compared to a large controlled cohort study, such as KEYNOTE-040 trial(ORR:15 %) [31]. This difference could be due to two reasons. First, the majority of the study population (82.5 %) received pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapy, which was shown to have a higher ORR compared to pembrolizumab alone in our study and other clinical studies [32,33]. Second, 73.2 % of untreated patients with local advanced stage received ICI as a neoadjuvant therapy in our cohort, which might have attributed to a high ORR. Additionally, the clinical staging exhibited no significant correlation with patient prognosis or the outcomes of immune therapy. This lack of correlation could be attributed to the predominance of locally advanced or recurrent/metastatic patients in the study, potentially introducing a statistical bias.

In our univariate regression analysis, we observed that the higher NLR and lower PLR and MLR in pretreatment were associated with a higher likelihood of immunotherapy response. Previous studies reported that the levels of NLR, PLR, and MLR were indicative of host inflammation and were associated with a poorer prognosis and cancer risk in various types of tumors [[34], [35], [36]]. What's more, studies showed that the basal and one-month variations in blood cell levels could strongly predict the efficacy of ICI treatment [37]. In our study, it was interesting to find that the increase of NLR and the decrease of MLR after the ICI treatment, suggesting a poor immune response, whereas a increase of PLR predicted a better immunotherapy benefit.

Based on the significance of the above markers in guiding immunotherapy response, we developed a MPTC model which integrated clinical parameters and blood inflammatory markers to identify patients likely to respond to immunotherapy, leveraging the significance of these markers in guiding therapeutic response. Our model surpassed the classical CPS marker in predictive efficiency (AUC: 0.614 vs 0.877). Although CPS did not show a significant correlation with the immune response in our study, it is a commonly used clinical marker with implications for assessment of immunotherapy response in various cancers. By contrasting the predictive efficacy of CPS as a standalone biomarker with our MPTC model, we aim to emphasize the critical importance of multi-parameter models in clinical decision-making. These integrated models, which incorporate diverse biomarkers, can lead to more precise predictions. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that patients with low model scores exhibited a significantly worse prognosis, compared to those with high scores. Conversely, when examining progression-free survival (PFS) within the CPS subgroup, no statistically significant differences were observed. These findings suggested that the MPTC model offers a more accurate prediction of clinical immunotherapy response and improved prognostic capabilities.

There are several limitations to our study that should be acknowledged. Firstly, this was a single-institution retrospective study with a relatively small sample size and a short follow-up period. Secondly, our model validation was performed using internal validation through bootstrap analysis, rather than through external cohort validation. To address these limitations, future research should include larger-scale, multicenter prospective studies that can replicate and validate our findings.

## Conclusions

In conclusion, we developed and internally validated a MPTC model based on the clinical parameters and blood inflammatory markers in patients with local advanced or R/M HNSCC receiving the ICI as the neoadjuvant therapy or first-line therapy. With the economical and readily available markers, this model can be easily assessed by clinical practice to help made decisions for ICI treatment and evaluate the duration and endpoint of immunotherapy for patients with HNSCC.
